amendments.rule: **A verbless clause with a prepositional predicate takes its supplied copula on the preposition.** Rule 20 supplies the copula from the construction; where the predicate is a prepositional phrase, the copula joins the preposition heading that phrase and the unit heads on the preposition — `בְכַפֵּיהֶם` → *is in their hands*, `בִמְסִלּוֹתָם` → *are in their paths*, `אִתָּנוּ` → *are with us*, `עָלֶיךָ` → *is upon thee*. **A directional predicate whose relation is carried by a directive `he` rather than by a preposition is read on the same terms.** Rule 32 makes such a `he` its own aligned unit by rule 11 wherever the ASV writes a word of its own for it, so where that directional phrase is the predicate of a verbless clause the construction-supplied copula joins the `he`'s unit and that unit heads on the word written for the direction, discontinuous around the noun under rule 25: `דֶּגֶל מַחֲנֵה רְאוּבֵן תֵּימָנָה` → *On the south side shall be the standard of the camp of Reuben* gives *On … shall be* to the `he`, while `תֵּימָן` keeps *the south side*, headed on *south* under rule 31, and the construct chain keeps only its own English. Read the Hebrew for which side is the predicate, as this rule's closing paragraph and rule 20 both direct: a definite construct chain standing in such a clause is its subject, and the ASV's inversion of the English is not evidence against that. Two limits. Where the ASV writes no separate word for the `he` and the two share one unit under rule 30, there is no separate unit to carry the copula and it joins that one fused unit. And where a participial or other nominal phrase is the clause's subject, so that the directional phrase is not the predicate at all, rule 20 governs and the copula joins the nominal predicate instead — `וְהַחֹנִים קֵדְמָה מִזְרָחָה דֶּגֶל מַחֲנֵה יְהוּדָה` → *And those that encamp on the east side toward the sunrising shall be they of the standard of the camp of Judah* leaves the directive `he` its bare *on*. **A resultative prepositional predicate takes the ASV's supplied result or change frame on the same terms.** The preposition carries the relation that English expresses with the frame: `לְ` → *to be*, *shall be turned into*, *will be unto*, or *shalt become*. This is not rule 20's wholly supplied lexical verb, because removing the English frame removes the preposition's own result relation; any explicit Hebrew subject still takes the English subject pronoun separately. Head the preposition's unit on the English word carrying that relation — *to* in *to be*, *into* in *shall be turned into*, *unto* in *will be unto*, and *become* where no English preposition remains. The ordinary copular case is settled rather than a tie: the corpus reads it this way in 103 units across 39 chapters and never moves the copula onto the object noun instead. It is settled; the note need not hedge it. **A relational verb the ASV writes where a copula would stand goes the same way.** Where a possessive or belonging `לְ` heads the predicate and the ASV renders the clause with a verb of belonging rather than a bare copula — `אֲשֶׁר לַבָּיִת` → *which belonged to the house* — that verb is part of the preposition's own rendering and joins its unit, headed on the English preposition written for it. It is not rule 20's wholly supplied lexical verb: drop the verb and the preposition's relation is what has gone and nothing else, which is the subtraction test rule 43 applies to the same clause written with *had*. Where the ASV does write *had* or *have*, rule 43 governs; where it writes a bare copula, the first sentence of this rule does. **But every sentence above governs a phrase for which the ASV has written an English preposition, and says nothing about one for which it has written none.** Where the ASV spends no word on the preposition's own relation and instead writes that relation inside the following word — a possessive or belonging `לְ` rendered as an English genitive, `לַיהוָה` → *is Jehovah's* — rule 30's one-rendering condition is met: one English word carries both the relation and the lexeme, and the preposition shares that word's unit, headed on the word carrying the lexeme. The construction's copula then joins that one fused unit, exactly as it joins `לִפְנֵי` → *was before* under rule 30, which states that a copula the construction hands to the whole of an expression does not defeat the condition. Test by the subtraction rules 16, 30 and 43 use: drop the copula and ask whether the preposition has lost a rendering of its own or only the clause has lost the tense English writes for it. Where only the clause is diminished, the preposition has no separate English and fuses; where an English preposition of its own remains — *is in their hands* — the first sentence of this rule governs and the copula stays with it. Do not reach for rule 2 to split the fused pair on the ground that the noun or name holds an English word of its own: that reasoning is rule 57's, where each of two nouns holds a word, and here the preposition holds none. The corpus reads `לְ` + the divine name this way in six units across five chapters — *is Jehovah's*, *shall be Jehovah's*, *am Jehovah's*, and a bare *Jehovah's* — and never splits a copula onto the preposition beside a separately aligned name. **And every sentence above governs a preposition that is itself the clause's predicate, never one heading an adjunct the ASV has merely placed the copula beside.** Where a nominal predicate stands in the verbless clause and a prepositional phrase modifies it, the copula and any dummy subject are rule 20's and join that nominal, whichever order the ASV writes the two in: `חֻקַּת עוֹלָם לְדֹרֹתֵיכֶם` → *it shall be a statute for ever throughout your generations* and `מֵאֵת בְּנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּרִית עוֹלָם` → *it is on the behalf of the children of Israel an everlasting covenant* are one construction, and both give the copula to the construct nominal, the second unit discontinuous around the fronted phrase under rule 25 while the preposition keeps only the English written for its own relation. Read the Hebrew clause for which side is the predicate rather than the English word order, exactly as rule 20 directs, since a phrase the ASV fronts puts the copula beside something that predicates nothing; and do not let a fused compound preposition draw the copula in under rule 30's one-rendering condition, which reaches a copula the construction hands to that expression and not one another morpheme is there to take. Where the clause writes no nominal predicate at all, nothing competes and the first sentence of this rule governs as before. **But a nominal standing beside a prepositional phrase is not a nominal predicate merely because the ASV writes the copula next to it.** Where the clause writes no subject but that one nominal, and the ASV writes no separate English subject for the clause either, the nominal is the clause's subject and the prepositional phrase is its predicate, so the copula stays on the preposition under this rule's first sentence — whichever order the ASV writes the two in, and however indefinite the English nominal is. `בְּפֶשַׁע שְׂפָתַיִם מוֹקֵשׁ רָע` → *In the transgression of the lips* ***is*** *a snare*, `בְּאֹרַח־צְדָקָה חַיִּים` → *In the way of righteousness* ***is*** *life*, `מִרְמָה בְּלֶב־חֹרְשֵׁי רָע` → *Deceit* ***is in*** *the heart of them that devise evil* and `וּלְיֹעֲצֵי שָׁלוֹם שִׂמְחָה` → *But* ***to*** *the counsellors of peace* ***is*** *joy* all put the copula on the preposition, and an indefinite *a snare* is no more a predicate than the definite construct chain the paragraph above calls a subject. What the preceding paragraph governs is a clause that has a subject of its own for the nominal to predicate of, which the ASV writes as a separate English subject — the *it* of *it shall be a statute for ever throughout your generations* and of *it is on the behalf of the children of Israel an everlasting covenant* — and a nominal that is itself the English subject of the copula in question is not that. So count the clause's nominals against the subjects the ASV writes, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s, before reading a phrase as an adjunct: where the only candidate subject is the nominal beside the preposition, the prepositional phrase is what predicates of it.
amendments.why: PRO.12 is almost entirely verbless bicola, and it analysed one construction two ways: PRO.12.4, 12.19, 12.20 and 12.28 gave the supplied copula to the preposition heading a locative or possessive predicate, while PRO.12.13 — `בְּפֶשַׁע שְׂפָתַיִם מוֹקֵשׁ רָע` → *In the transgression of the lips is a snare* — gave it to the following indefinite nominal under rule 20, though the clause is the same shape as PRO.12.28's `בְּאֹרַח־צְדָקָה חַיִּים` and the ASV writes both in the same English order. Rule 49 already told the reader to read the Hebrew for which side is the predicate and already ruled that a definite construct chain in such a clause is its subject, but its closing paragraph's adjunct carve-out could be read as covering any nominal the copula stands beside, which is what produced the split. The addition states the test rather than the outcome, and it is drawn so that both examples already in the rule — where the ASV writes a separate *it* subject — keep their existing analysis; the corpus figure of 103 prepositional-predicate units with the copula never moved onto the object noun is the precedent it rests on.

conventions: Proverbs 12 is almost entirely verbless bicola, and the chapter reads the supplied copula by which side of the Hebrew clause is the predicate rather than by the ASV's English order. Where a prepositional phrase is the predicate the copula joins that preposition under rule 49 — `כְּרָקָב בְּעַצְמוֹתָיו` → *is as rottenness* (12.4), `בְּפֶשַׁע שְׂפָתַיִם ... מוֹקֵשׁ` → *In ... is a snare* (12.13), `עַד־אַרְגִּיעָה` → *is ... for* (12.19), `בְּלֶב־חֹרְשֵׁי רָע` and `לְיֹעֲצֵי שָׁלוֹם` → *is in* and *to ... is* (12.20), `בְּאֹרַח־צְדָקָה` → *In ... is* (12.28). A bare or indefinite nominal standing beside such a phrase is the clause's subject, not its predicate, wherever the clause writes no other subject and the ASV writes no separate English subject for it. Where instead the predicate is a nominal or adjective with no preposition on it, the copula joins that word under rule 20 — 12.1, 12.5, 12.9, 12.10, 12.15, 12.18, 12.22, 12.27, 12.28b.

report: Checked all 28 verses end to end against the 37-lemma candidate table and the dump. One real split found: the placement of the construction-supplied copula in verbless clauses with a prepositional predicate. PRO.12.4 (`כְּ` → *is as*), 12.19 (`עַד` → *is for*), 12.20 (`בְּ` → *is in*, `לְ` → *to … is*) and 12.28 (`בְּ` → *In … is*) all follow rule 49; PRO.12.13 alone put *is* on the following nominal `מוֹקֵשׁ`, though its clause is the same shape as 12.28's and the ASV writes both in the same order. Patched PRO.12.13.

Candidates cleared as licensed by the source or by the ASV's own wording: the waw's *But*/*and*/*And* (rule 14 reads the connective off the ASV); `לְ` unrepresented at 12.8 versus *under* at 12.24 (rule 21's resultative `הָיָה לְ`, where 12.24's recasting does write a word for the preposition and 12.8's does not); `שָׂבֵעַ` as *shall have plenty of* (12.11) versus *shall be satisfied with* (12.14), both keeping the function word with the verb under rules 44 and 33; `דֶּרֶךְ` as *the way* (12.15, 12.24, 12.26) versus *in* (12.28), which is rule 19's construct-preposition case and passes its subtraction test; `חָסֵר` at 12.9 and 12.11; the suffixes left unrepresented at 12.7, 12.9 and 12.16, each under a named rule (50, 43, 25).

The four `added` units were re-examined and stand: the italic *But* of 12.5 (the verse writes no waw at all), *fruit* of 12.12 (rule 44's supplied object that does not carry `נָתַן`'s lexeme), the restrictive *but* of 12.19 (`עַד` already holds *for*), and *thereof* of 12.28 (no possessive morpheme in the phrase).

BSB disagreements (12.7 `ם`, 12.8 `לָ`, 12.9 `וֹ`, 12.16 `וֹ`): none is an error. Each is a morpheme this project marks unrepresented under a rule BSB does not share — rule 50's unrendered suffix on `אֵינָם`, rule 21's resultative `לְ` in *shall be despised*, rule 43's suffix where the ASV writes no subject pronoun beside *hath*, and rule 25's suffix whose possessive force the written `אֱוִיל` already carries in *A fool's*. Nothing was changed to improve the rate.
Recorded one convention (copula placement across the chapter's verbless bicola) and one amendment to rule 49 stating the test that would have prevented the split.
